Classical Substitution Ciphers

The Core Idea

A substitution technique is one in which the letters of plaintext are replaced by other letters, numbers, or symbols [cite: 31].

If the plaintext is viewed as a sequence of bits, substitution involves replacing plaintext bit patterns with ciphertext bit patterns [cite: 32].

The Caesar Cipher (Shift Cipher)

One of the simplest and most widely known encryption techniques [cite: 35]. It replaces each letter in the plaintext with a letter found by moving a certain number of positions down or up the alphabet [cite: 36, 39].

History: First attested use in military affairs was by Julius Caesar, described by him in the Gallic Wars [cite: 37].

Encryption Process Overview

  • Plaintext: The original message you want to encrypt [cite: 40].
  • Key: The number of positions each letter will be shifted [cite: 41].
  • Ciphertext: The resulting encrypted message [cite: 41].
Class Work Example: The plaintext 'howdy' (positions 7, 14, 22, 3, 24) encrypted using key 'f' (a shift of 5) becomes 'MTBID' [cite: 79].

Mathematical Representation

Caesar Cipher Formula

The algorithm uses modulo (clock) arithmetic. When you reach Z, you go back to A and start again [cite: 76, 77]. Modulo 26 implies that when you reach 26, you use 0 instead [cite: 78].

C = E(k, p) = (p + k) mod 26 [cite: 79]

Where C = Ciphertext, E = Encryption, k = Key, p = Plaintext.

Symmetric Encryption Model

Plaintext (X)
+ Key (K) ➔
Algorithm (E)
➔
Ciphertext (Y)

Requirements for Secure Use

There are two primary requirements for the secure use of symmetric encryption [cite: 50]:

  • A strong encryption algorithm [cite: 50]. Even if someone knows how the encryption method works, they shouldn't be able to decode the message without the secret key [cite: 80].
  • A secret key known only to the sender and receiver [cite: 50]. We don't need to keep the encryption method itself a secret, only the key [cite: 81].

Mathematically, we have: Y = E(K, X) for encryption, and X = D(K, Y) for decryption [cite: 50].

Breaking the Caesar Cipher

Why Caesar is Not Secure

The Caesar cipher is not secure in modern cryptography. Its weaknesses include [cite: 52]:

  • Limited Key Space: There are only 25 possible keys [cite: 52].
  • Brute-Force Vulnerability: An attacker can easily try all possible shifts to break the cipher [cite: 52].
  • Letter Frequency Analysis: It preserves letter frequency. In English, letters like 'E' and 'T' appear more frequently, and these patterns can be exploited [cite: 52, 53].
  • Predictable Shifting: Once the key is discovered, the entire cipher is exposed [cite: 53].
  • No Modern Safeguards: It does not provide confidentiality, integrity, or authentication [cite: 53].

Improving the Cipher

The Vigenère Cipher

Addresses Caesar's weaknesses by using a keyword to vary the shift amount at each position in the plaintext [cite: 56].

Example: Encrypting "HELLO" with keyword "KEY". The keyword repeats to "KEYKE". 'H' shifted by 'K' (10) becomes 'R'. 'E' shifted by 'E' (4) becomes 'I'. The final ciphertext is "RIJVS" [cite: 89, 90, 91].

Modern Algorithms

Algorithms like AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) use much more complex and secure methods for encryption [cite: 57].

Monoalphabetic Ciphers

Arbitrary Substitution

Because the Caesar cipher only has 25 possible keys, it is far from secure [cite: 92]. To make encryption much stronger and dramatically increase the key space, we use arbitrary substitution, where the translation alphabet can be any permutation of the 26 alphabetic characters [cite: 59, 93].

What is a Permutation?

A permutation is a specific arrangement of a set of elements where each element appears exactly once [cite: 60]. For example, the permutations of S={a,b,c} are abc, acb, bac, bca, cab, cba [cite: 61].

In general, there are n! permutations of a set of n elements [cite: 95].

The Massive Key Space

Since the English alphabet has 26 letters, the total number of keys is 26! [cite: 68].

26! ≈ 4 × 1026 keys [cite: 68]

This is 10 orders of magnitude greater than the key space for the DES standard [cite: 107].

Language Redundancy & Cryptanalysis

The Flaw in Monoalphabetic Ciphers

Even with 4 × 1026 keys, you might think it is secure, but that would be WRONG! [cite: 68]. The problem is language characteristics [cite: 68]. Monoalphabetic substitution does not sufficiently obscure the underlying language characteristics [cite: 107].

Example: If the word "HELLO" appears often in a message, "H" will always be replaced by the same letter, and "E" by another. A smart attacker can figure out the message by looking for these patterns [cite: 69].

Letter Frequencies

Human languages are redundant, and letters are not equally commonly used [cite: 71]. Basic cryptanalysis involves counting relative frequencies of letters and noting patterns [cite: 112].

  • Most Common: 'E' is by far the most common letter in English [cite: 71].
  • High Frequency: T, R, N, I, O, A, S [cite: 71].
  • Rare Letters: Z, J, K, Q, X [cite: 71].

Advanced Pattern Matching

Cryptanalysts don't just look at single letters. They also analyze multi-letter combinations to break the cipher:

  • Digrams: Common two-letter combinations [cite: 115].
  • Trigrams: Common three-letter combinations [cite: 115].

Knowledge Check

1. How many possible keys exist in a standard Caesar Cipher? [cite: 52]
Correct! Since shifting by 26 brings you back to the same alphabet, there are only 25 possible keys [cite: 52].
2. What is the mathematical formula for the Caesar Cipher encryption? [cite: 79]
Correct! The formula uses addition and modulo 26 arithmetic [cite: 79].
3. Why is the Monoalphabetic Cipher considered insecure despite having 4 × 10²⁶ keys? [cite: 107]
Correct! It is vulnerable to frequency analysis because it preserves the redundancy of the human language [cite: 107, 71].
4. Which of the following is the most common letter in the English language? [cite: 71]
Correct! 'E' is by far the most common letter in English [cite: 71].
